newsitem.title: UK: Few survivors seen in forex future - BOT-Mitsubishi.
newsitem.headline: Few survivors seen in forex future - BOT-Mitsubishi.

text.p: Life in the world of foreign exchange is set to get even tougher in 1997 and beyond as competitive forces continue to bite, the senior forex team at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in London told Reuters in an interview.
The team highlighted the progress and acceptance of electronic broking and the drive for centralised, cost-saving forex operations as whittling the number of major currency players down even further.

"The competitiveness is getting hard and we think only 10-15 major banks can survive this industry in time to come," said Masamichi Yasuda, chief of foreign exchange trading at BOT-Mitsubishi. "Not only for forex but also all market products. People will have to supply all products to meet every customer's demand."

In Japan, this has already begun with small- to medium-sized banks becoming less involved with the interbank market, becoming customers themselves to the larger banks. And as Japan's foreign exchange deregulation measures get into full swing, this consolidation is expected to continue.

One of the significant factors of this streamlining is the acceptance of electronic broking. The migration to this trading platform comes from customers' attraction to the ever-tightening spreads and fast execution as well as the relatively low costs.

"You now only have two electronic broking companies to deal with that are actually covering all the major currencies," said Martin Ely, head of proprietary trading at BOT-Mitsubishi. "So it's easy for banks to coordinate electronic broking, keeping costs down."
However, while banks' customers become the winners in this deal, the banks themselves are seeing profit margins eroded with tightening spreads.

"It has caused market spreads to customers to become much tighter and much more competitive," said Ely. "And it's at breakneck speed at the moment with it getting so fast and spreads tighter which obviously eats into the profit margin of the banks concerned."
Junpei Yamamoto, head of foreign exchange at BOT-Mitsubishi in London, also sees this growth of electronic broking having a knock-on effect on London as the world's centrepiece for currency trade.

"I think the London market will be the main market for foreign exchange for maybe the next 10 years. But many people take part in the London market and such a market needs price action," says Yamamoto.
"Electronic broking makes price action small, so I think the London market will not be as attractive as it is now."

Another effect already becoming more widespread is the reduction in forex staffing, which the BOT-Mitsubishi team attributes mainly to the advance of technology rather than a decline in business. And as technology continues to improve, they see this trend continuing.

Yasuda sees this in the centralisation of forex operations. Where some banks used to run five or six local foreign exchange centres around the globe, now it can be done from one or two central operations, he says.
The advent of a single European currency is also at the forefront of the industry's focus, but Yasuda is relatively sanguine about its impact.
"There should be some effect on the FX market, but as far as we are concerned and what the BIS survey showed two years ago, the share of European currencies in the global market was 10-15 percent."
"So the effect is not so big that we can't compensate with the development of emerging currency markets."
On emerging currencies, they see the Asian markets offering more opportunities than those in Eastern Europe.
"They've been going a lot longer, people know more about them, and people can go back three or ten years and see what has been steady growth," says Ely.

Volatility, notably absent from 1996, has already made a return at start of this year and is expected to continue, particularly amid overhanging nervousness of the timetable and participants in Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).
Yasuda is optimistic the currency derivatives business will increase as a result and as customers increase their asset hedging operations for the start of EMU and the onset of the euro.
Overall, the BOT-Mitsubishi team see survival in the forex market in the trend towards centralisation, with banks offering a range of products for the customer -- a "one-stop shop".
"We've seen over the last few years corporates reduce their core banks and that's probably going to be an ongoing situation," says Ely.
"You have to be more of a supermarket rather than offer boutique type products which will allow you to survive."
